description: Energy stores and transfers, work done, gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, and power.
content_html:
Energy Stores and the Conservation of Energy

The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred between stores. In any closed system, total energy before a process equals total energy after. Energy that seems to ‘disappear’ has been dissipated — spread into less useful thermal energy in the surroundings.

Energy can be stored in different ways: kinetic (moving objects), gravitational potential (objects at height), elastic potential (stretched or compressed objects), chemical (fuels, food, batteries), thermal (hot objects), magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear. Energy transfers between these stores via heating, radiation, electrical current or mechanical work.

Key Fact

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It transfers between stores — kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, chemical, thermal, magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear. Dissipated energy is wasted as thermal energy in the surroundings.

Work Done

When a force moves an object through a distance, work is done. Work done equals the amount of energy transferred. The equation is:

$$W = F \times d$$

where \(W\) is work done in joules (J), \(F\) is the applied force in newtons (N) and \(d\) is the distance moved in the direction of the force in metres (m). One joule of work is done when a force of 1 N moves an object through 1 m.

Work done on an object equals the energy transferred to it. When you push a box across a rough floor, work is done against friction and energy is transferred to the thermal stores of the box and floor. This is why friction causes objects to warm up during sliding — kinetic energy is continuously converted to thermal energy in the surroundings.

Gravitational Potential Energy

When an object is raised against gravity, energy is stored in its gravitational potential energy (GPE) store:

$$GPE = m \times g \times h$$

where \(m\) is mass in kg, \(g\) is the gravitational field strength (10 N/kg for OCR calculations) and \(h\) is the height gained in metres. For example, lifting a 4 kg book to a shelf 1.5 m high: \(GPE = 4 \times 10 \times 1.5 = 60\) J.

Kinetic Energy

Any moving object has kinetic energy (KE):

$$KE = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2$$

where \(m\) is mass in kg and \(v\) is speed in m/s. Notice that KE depends on \(v^2\) — doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy. This explains why stopping distances increase so sharply at higher speeds: a car at 30 m/s has four times the KE of one at 15 m/s and requires four times the braking distance.

A rollercoaster car of mass 500 kg is raised to a height of 40 m before being released.

Step 1 — GPE at the top: \(GPE = 500 \times 10 \times 40 = 200{,}000\) J = 200 kJ.

Step 2 — KE at the bottom (assuming no friction): by conservation of energy, all GPE converts to KE. \(KE = 200{,}000\) J.

Step 3 — Speed at the bottom: \(200{,}000 = \frac{1}{2} \times 500 \times v^2\) → \(v^2 = \frac{200{,}000 \times 2}{500} = 800\) → \(v = \sqrt{800} \approx 28.3\) m/s.

In practice, friction and air resistance would dissipate some energy as thermal energy, so the actual speed at the bottom would be lower than 28 m/s.

Key Fact

Work done: \(W = F \times d\) (joules). Gravitational PE: \(GPE = m \times g \times h\) (joules). Kinetic energy: \(KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\) (joules). Doubling speed quadruples KE.

Power

Power measures how quickly energy is transferred. The equations are:

$$P = \frac{E}{t} \quad \text{and} \quad P = \frac{W}{t}$$

where \(P\) is power in watts (W), \(E\) or \(W\) is energy transferred or work done in joules (J), and \(t\) is time in seconds (s). One watt equals one joule per second. A device with a higher power rating transfers the same amount of energy in less time — a 2000 W kettle boils water in half the time of a 1000 W kettle.

No energy transfer is perfectly efficient — some energy is always dissipated as thermal energy. Efficiency is calculated as:

$$\text{Efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{total input energy}}$$

A result of 0.7 means 70% efficient (30% wasted). For example, a motor that receives 500 J of electrical energy and does 350 J of useful mechanical work: efficiency = \(\frac{350}{500} = 0.70\) = 70%. The remaining 150 J is dissipated as heat and sound.

Engineers reduce waste energy through lubrication (less friction), streamlining (less air resistance), thermal insulation (less heat loss) and using more efficient technologies such as LED lighting instead of traditional incandescent bulbs.

Elastic potential energy is stored when a spring or elastic material is deformed:

$$EPE = \frac{1}{2} \times k \times e^2$$

where \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m and \(e\) is the extension in metres. Like KE, EPE depends on the square of the deformation — doubling the extension stores four times the energy. This equation applies only within the limit of proportionality, where force and extension are directly proportional (Hooke’s Law).
exam_tip_html: For calculations, always write the equation first, substitute correctly and show every step of working. A common error in KE calculations is forgetting to halve the product \(mv^2\) — write out the fraction explicitly. When calculating GPE, use \(g = 10\) N/kg (the OCR standard value). The more precise value is 9.8 N/kg but OCR mark schemes use 10. For efficiency, check that you are dividing useful output by total input (not the other way round). Remember: power is the rate of energy transfer, not total energy.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Energy is conserved — it transfers between stores (kinetic, GPE, thermal, chemical etc.) and is never created or destroyed. Dissipated energy becomes waste heat in the surroundings.
  • Work done \(W = Fd\); gravitational PE \(= mgh\); kinetic energy \(= \frac{1}{2}mv^2\). All measured in joules. Doubling speed quadruples KE.
  • Power \(P = E/t\) or \(W/t\), measured in watts. Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. No device is 100% efficient; engineers reduce waste via lubrication, streamlining and insulation.

practice_questions.text: State the equation for gravitational potential energy and identify the unit of each quantity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: GPE = m × g × h; m in kg, g in N/kg, h in metres, GPE in joules.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to the energy stored in a compressed spring when it is released and propels a ball upwards.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: elastic potential energy in the spring is transferred to kinetic energy of the ball as it is released. 1 mark: as the ball rises, kinetic energy is transferred to gravitational potential energy (some is also dissipated as thermal energy due to air resistance).

practice_questions.text: A cyclist of total mass 70 kg (including the bicycle) travels at 8 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy of the cyclist. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct equation KE = ½ × m × v². 1 mark: correct substitution KE = ½ × 70 × 8². 1 mark: v² = 64 correctly evaluated, giving KE = ½ × 70 × 64 = 2240. 1 mark: correct answer 2240 J with correct unit.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a car travelling at 30 m/s requires a much greater braking distance than the same car travelling at 15 m/s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: states that KE = ½mv² so KE depends on v²; the car at 30 m/s has four times the KE of the car at 15 m/s (since speed is doubled, KE is quadrupled); braking force is constant so the car must travel four times the distance to dissipate four times the KE. Secure: states doubling speed quadruples KE and therefore quadruples braking distance. Developing: states higher speed means more KE and longer braking distance without using the v² relationship. Emerging: simply states faster speed means harder to stop, no reference to KE.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following is the correct unit for power?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: Watts (W). Distractors: Joules (J); Newtons (N); Joules per metre (J/m).

practice_questions.text: An electric motor lifts a 150 N load through a height of 3 m in 5 seconds. The motor uses 1200 J of electrical energy during this time. Calculate the efficiency of the motor and evaluate one way in which the wasted energy could be reduced.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: calculates useful work done = 150 × 3 = 450 J; calculates efficiency = 450 ÷ 1200 = 0.375 = 37.5%; identifies that wasted energy is likely heat due to friction in the motor; suggests lubrication to reduce friction and improve efficiency; recognises 62.5% of input energy is wasted and evaluates whether improving efficiency is worthwhile. Secure: correct efficiency calculation with one improvement method identified. Developing: calculates useful work correctly but makes an error in efficiency equation, or efficiency is correct but no evaluation of improvement. Emerging: identifies useful output and input energy but cannot calculate efficiency correctly.

knowledge_checks.q: A 2 kg ball is raised to a height of 5 m. Using g = 10 N/kg, what is its gravitational potential energy?
A device receives 800 J of energy and transfers 600 J usefully. What is its efficiency?

When a spring is compressed and then released, energy transfers from _____ potential energy to kinetic energy.

glossary_terms.definition: The principle that energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred from one store to another; the total energy of a closed system remains constant.
Energy spread out into less useful forms, usually thermal energy in the surroundings; also called wasted energy.
The energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force, measured in joules.
The energy stored in an object because of its height above a reference level, calculated using GPE = m × g × h.
The energy an object has because of its motion, calculated using KE = ½ × m × v².
The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done, measured in watts (W) where 1 W = 1 J/s.
The proportion of total input energy that is usefully transferred, calculated as useful output energy divided by total input energy.
The energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring or elastic material, calculated using EPE = ½ × k × e².
